paragraphs: Muse, tell me about the clever hero who wandered the world after he destroyed the famous city of Troy. He visited many cities and learned how many different peoples live. At sea he suffered terribly, fighting to save his own life and bring his men home. But whatever he did, he couldn’t save them. They doomed themselves through sheer foolishness by eating the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion, and so the god made sure they never got home. Tell me about all of it, daughter of Jove, from wherever you know it.

By now everyone who had escaped death in battle or at sea had gotten safely home, except Ulysses. Though he longed to return to his wife and country, he was held captive by the goddess Calypso, who had him in a large cave and wanted to marry him. But as the years passed, the gods decided it was time for him to go back to Ithaca. Even then, when he was among his own people, his troubles would not be over. Still, all the gods had by now begun to pity him except Neptune, who kept persecuting him without pause and wouldn’t let him get home.

Neptune, though, had gone off to visit the Ethiopians, who live at the end of the world, split into two groups, one facing west and the other east. He had gone there to accept a sacrifice of a hundred sheep and oxen and was enjoying himself at his festival. Meanwhile the other gods gathered in the house of Olympian Jove, and the father of gods and men spoke first. At that moment he was thinking of Aegisthus, who had been killed by Agamemnon’s son Orestes, so he said to the other gods:

“Look how men blame us gods for what is, after all, nothing but their own foolishness. Look at Aegisthus. He had to seduce Agamemnon’s wife, a wicked thing to do, and then kill Agamemnon, though he knew it would mean his own death. I sent Mercury to warn him not to do either of these things, since Orestes would be sure to take revenge when he grew up and wanted to come home. Mercury told him this with the best of intentions, but he wouldn’t listen, and now he has paid for everything in full.”

Then Minerva said, “Father, son of Saturn, King of kings, Aegisthus got what he deserved, and so would anyone else who does what he did. But Aegisthus is beside the point. It’s Ulysses my heart bleeds for when I think of his sufferings on that lonely island in the sea, far from all his friends, poor man. It’s an island covered with forest, right in the middle of the sea, and a goddess lives there, the daughter of the magician Atlas, who looks after the bottom of the ocean and carries the great columns that hold heaven and earth apart. This daughter of Atlas has got hold of poor, unhappy Ulysses and keeps trying, with every kind of flattery, to make him forget his home, so that he’s tired of life and thinks of nothing but seeing the smoke from his own chimneys again. And you, sir, take no notice of this, yet when Ulysses was before Troy, didn’t he win your favor with many a burnt offering? Why do you keep on being so angry with him?”

And Jove said, “My child, what are you talking about? How could I forget Ulysses, who is more capable than any man on earth and more generous in his offerings to the immortal gods who live in heaven? But remember that Neptune is still furious with Ulysses for blinding the eye of Polyphemus, king of the Cyclopes. Polyphemus is Neptune’s son by the nymph Thoosa, daughter of the sea king Phorcys, so though Neptune won’t kill Ulysses outright, he torments him by preventing him from getting home. Still, let’s put our heads together and see how we can help him return. Then Neptune will calm down, because if we’re all of one mind, he can hardly stand against us.”

And Minerva said, “Father, son of Saturn, King of kings, if the gods now mean for Ulysses to get home, we should first send Mercury to the island of Ogygia to tell Calypso that we’ve made up our minds and that he is to return. In the meantime I’ll go to Ithaca to put some courage into Ulysses’ son Telemachus. I’ll encourage him to call the Achaeans to an assembly and speak out against the suitors of his mother Penelope, who keep eating up his sheep and oxen by the dozen. I’ll also take him to Sparta and Pylos to see if he can hear anything about his dear father’s return, because that will make people speak well of him.”

With these words she strapped on her glittering golden sandals, imperishable ones, with which she can fly like the wind over land or sea. She took up her formidable bronze-tipped spear, so stout and sturdy and strong, with which she crushes the ranks of heroes who have displeased her, and darted down from the highest peaks of Olympus. At once she was in Ithaca, at the gateway of Ulysses’ house, disguised as a visitor, Mentes, chief of the Taphians, holding a bronze spear in her hand. There she found the arrogant suitors sitting on hides from the oxen they had killed and eaten, playing checkers in front of the house. Servants and pages bustled around waiting on them, some mixing wine with water in the mixing bowls, some wiping down the tables with wet sponges and setting them out again, and some carving great quantities of meat.

Telemachus saw her long before anyone else did. He was sitting gloomily among the suitors, thinking about his brave father and how he would send them flying out of the house if he were ever to come home again and be honored as in days gone by. Brooding like this as he sat among them, he caught sight of Minerva and went straight to the gate, annoyed that a stranger should be kept waiting for admission. He took her right hand in his and asked her to give him her spear. “Welcome to our house,” he said, “and when you’ve had something to eat, you can tell us what you’ve come for.”

He led the way as he spoke, and Minerva followed him. When they were inside, he took her spear and set it in the spear rack against a strong pillar, along with the many other spears of his unfortunate father. He led her to a richly decorated seat, over which he threw a fine cloth. There was a footstool for her feet, too, and he set another seat close by for himself, away from the suitors, so that she wouldn’t be annoyed by their noise and insolence while she ate, and so that he could ask her more freely about his father.

A maidservant then brought them water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it into a silver basin for them to wash their hands, and she set a clean table beside them. A senior servant brought them bread and offered them many good things from what the house had to give. The carver brought them plates of all kinds of meat and set golden cups beside them, and a manservant brought wine and poured it out for them.

Then the suitors came in and took their places on the benches and seats. At once servants poured water over their hands, maids went around with the bread baskets, pages filled the mixing bowls with wine and water, and they helped themselves to the good things in front of them. As soon as they’d had enough to eat and drink, they wanted music and dancing, which are the crowning touches of a banquet, so a servant brought a lyre to Phemius, whom they forced to sing for them. As soon as he touched his lyre and began to sing, Telemachus spoke quietly to Minerva, with his head close to hers so that no one could hear.

“I hope, sir,” he said, “you won’t be offended by what I’m about to say. Singing comes cheap to those who don’t have to pay for it, and all this is done at the expense of a man whose bones lie rotting in some wilderness or being ground to powder in the surf. If these men saw my father come back to Ithaca, they’d pray for faster legs rather than fatter purses, because money wouldn’t save them. But he, alas, has met a bad fate, and even when people do sometimes say he’s coming, we no longer pay attention. We’ll never see him again. And now, sir, tell me, and tell me truly, who you are and where you come from. Tell me about your town and your parents, what kind of ship you came in, how your crew brought you to Ithaca, and what country they said they were from, because you can’t have come by land. Tell me also truly, because I want to know, are you a stranger to this house, or were you here in my father’s time? In the old days we had many visitors, because my father traveled a lot himself.”

And Minerva answered, “I’ll tell you truthfully and in detail. I’m Mentes, son of Anchialus, and I’m king of the Taphians. I’ve come here with my ship and crew on a voyage to people who speak a foreign language, headed for Temesa with a cargo of iron, and I’ll bring back copper. As for my ship, it lies over there off the open country, away from the town, in the harbor of Rheithron, under the wooded mountain Neritum. Our fathers were friends before us, as old Laertes will tell you if you go and ask him. They say, however, that he never comes to town now and lives by himself in the country, living poorly, with an old woman to look after him and get his dinner when he comes in tired from pottering about his vineyard. They told me your father was home again, and that’s why I came, but it seems the gods are still holding him back, because he isn’t dead yet, nor on the mainland. It’s more likely he’s on some sea-bound island in the middle of the ocean, or a prisoner among savages who are keeping him against his will. I’m no prophet and know very little about omens, but I speak as it’s been put into my mind from heaven, and I assure you he won’t be away much longer. He’s a man of such resourcefulness that even if he were in iron chains, he’d find some way of getting home. But tell me, and tell me truthfully, can Ulysses really have such a fine-looking fellow for a son? You really are wonderfully like him around the head and eyes, because we were close friends before he sailed for Troy, where the flower of all the Greeks went too. Since then we’ve never seen each other.”

“My mother,” answered Telemachus, “tells me I’m Ulysses’ son, but it’s a wise child that knows his own father. I wish I were the son of a man who had grown old on his own estates, because, since you ask, there’s no more unlucky man under heaven than the one they say is my father.”

And Minerva said, “There’s no danger of your family dying out yet, while Penelope has such a fine son as you. But tell me, and tell me truthfully, what is the meaning of all this feasting, and who are these people? What’s it all about? Are you having a banquet, or is there a wedding in the family? Because no one seems to have brought any food of his own. And the guests, how appallingly they’re behaving! What an uproar they make all over the house! It would disgust any respectable person who came near them.”

“Sir,” said Telemachus, “as for your question, as long as my father was here, all was well with us and with the house, but the gods in their displeasure have willed it otherwise and have hidden him away more completely than any mortal man was ever hidden. I could have borne it better if he were dead, if he had fallen with his men before Troy, or died among friends when his days of fighting were over, because then the Greeks would have built a mound over his ashes, and I would have inherited his fame. But now the storm winds have snatched him away, we don’t know where. He’s gone without leaving so much as a trace behind, and I inherit nothing but dismay. And the matter doesn’t end with grief for my father. Heaven has laid another kind of sorrow on me. The chiefs from all our islands, Dulichium, Same, and the wooded island of Zacynthus, as well as all the leading men of Ithaca itself, are eating up my house on the pretext of courting my mother, who won’t say flatly that she won’t marry, nor bring the matter to an end. So they’re ruining my estate, and before long they’ll do the same to me.”

“Is that so?” exclaimed Minerva. “Then you really do need Ulysses home again. Give him a helmet, a shield, and a couple of spears, and if he’s the man he was when I first knew him in our house, drinking and making merry, he’d soon lay hands on these rascally suitors if he stood once more on his own threshold. He was then coming from Ephyra, where he’d gone to beg poison for his arrows from Ilus, son of Mermerus. Ilus feared the ever-living gods and wouldn’t give him any, but my father gave him some, because he was very fond of him. If Ulysses is the man he was then, these suitors will have a short reckoning and a sorry wedding.

“But there! It’s for heaven to decide whether he’ll return and take his revenge in his own house or not. I do urge you, though, to start trying to get rid of these suitors at once. Take my advice: call the Greek heroes to an assembly tomorrow morning, lay your case before them, and call on heaven to witness it. Tell the suitors to go away, each to his own home, and if your mother’s mind is set on marrying again, let her go back to her father, who will find her a husband and give her all the marriage gifts a daughter so dear can expect. As for yourself, let me persuade you to take the best ship you can get, with a crew of twenty men, and go in search of your father, who has been missing so long. Someone may tell you something, or (and people often hear things this way) some message from heaven may guide you. First go to Pylos and ask Nestor. From there go on to Sparta and visit Menelaus, because he was the last of the Greeks to get home. If you hear that your father is alive and on his way home, you can put up with the waste these suitors cause for another twelve months. If, on the other hand, you hear that he’s dead, come home at once, perform his funeral rites with all due ceremony, build a mound in his memory, and let your mother marry again. Then, when you’ve done all this, think carefully about how, by fair means or foul, you can kill these suitors in your own house. You’re too old to plead childhood any longer. Haven’t you heard how people are singing the praises of Orestes for killing his father’s murderer, Aegisthus? You’re a fine, smart-looking fellow. Show your mettle, then, and make a name for yourself in story. Now, though, I have to go back to my ship and my crew, who will be impatient if I keep them waiting any longer. Think it over for yourself, and remember what I’ve said to you.”

“Sir,” answered Telemachus, “it’s been very kind of you to talk to me like this, as though I were your own son, and I’ll do everything you say. I know you want to get on with your voyage, but stay a little longer until you’ve had a bath and refreshed yourself. I’ll then give you a present, and you can go on your way rejoicing. I’ll give you something of great beauty and value, a keepsake such as only dear friends give each other.”

Minerva answered, “Don’t try to keep me, because I want to be on my way at once. As for any gift you’d like to give me, keep it until I come again, and I’ll take it home with me. You can give me a very fine one, and I’ll give you one of equal value in return.”

With these words she flew away like a bird into the air, but she had given Telemachus courage and made him think about his father more than ever. He felt the change, wondered at it, and realized the stranger had been a god, so he went straight to where the suitors were sitting.

Phemius was still singing, and his listeners sat spellbound in silence as he told the sad tale of the return from Troy and the troubles Minerva had brought on the Greeks. Penelope, daughter of Icarius, heard his song from her room upstairs and came down the great staircase, not alone but attended by two of her maids. When she reached the suitors, she stood by one of the pillars that held up the roof of the hall, with a modest maid on either side of her. She held a veil in front of her face and was weeping bitterly.

“Phemius,” she cried, “you know many other deeds of gods and heroes, the kind poets love to celebrate. Sing the suitors one of those, and let them drink their wine in silence, but stop this sad tale, because it breaks my sorrowful heart and reminds me of my lost husband, whom I mourn without ceasing, and whose name was great all over Greece and middle Argos.”

“Mother,” answered Telemachus, “let the bard sing what he likes. Bards don’t make the evils they sing about. It’s Jove, not they, who makes them, and who sends good or bad fortune on mankind as he pleases. This fellow means no harm by singing about the ill-fated return of the Greeks, because people always applaud the newest songs most warmly. Make up your mind and bear it. Ulysses is not the only man who never came back from Troy. Many another went down as well as he. Go, then, into the house and busy yourself with your daily duties, your loom, your spindle, and directing your servants, because speech is a man’s business, and mine above all others, since I’m master here.”

She went back into the house, wondering, and laid her son’s words to heart. Then, going upstairs with her maids to her room, she mourned her dear husband until Minerva poured sweet sleep over her eyes. But the suitors were noisy throughout the covered hall, and each one prayed that he might be her bedfellow.

Then Telemachus spoke. “Shameless and insolent suitors,” he cried, “let us feast at our pleasure now, and let there be no brawling, because it’s rare to hear a man with such a divine voice as Phemius has. But in the morning meet me in full assembly so that I can give you formal notice to leave and feast at one another’s houses in turn, at your own expense. If, on the other hand, you choose to keep sponging off one man, heaven help me, Jove will settle accounts with you in full, and when you fall in my father’s house there will be no one to avenge you.”

The suitors bit their lips as they heard him and marveled at the boldness of his speech. Then Antinous, son of Eupeithes, said, “The gods seem to have given you lessons in bluster and big talk. May Jove never make you chief in Ithaca as your father was before you.”

Telemachus answered, “Antinous, don’t scold me. With the gods’ will, I’ll be chief too if I can. Is this the worst fate you can think of for me? It’s no bad thing to be a chief, because it brings both riches and honor. Still, now that Ulysses is dead, there are many great men in Ithaca, both old and young, and someone else might take the lead among them. Nevertheless, I will be chief in my own house and rule those whom Ulysses won for me.”

Then Eurymachus, son of Polybus, answered, “It’s for heaven to decide who will be chief among us, but you’ll be master in your own house and over your own possessions. No one, while there’s a man left in Ithaca, will do you violence or rob you. And now, my good fellow, I want to know about this stranger. What country does he come from? What family is he of, and where is his estate? Did he bring you news about your father’s return, or was he here on business of his own? He seemed a wealthy man, but he hurried off so suddenly that he was gone in a moment, before we could get to know him.”

“My father is dead and gone,” answered Telemachus, “and even if some rumor reaches me, I put no more faith in it now. My mother does sometimes send for a soothsayer and question him, but I pay no attention to his prophecies. As for the stranger, he was Mentes, son of Anchialus, chief of the Taphians, an old friend of my father’s.” But in his heart he knew it had been the goddess.

The suitors then went back to their singing and dancing until evening, but when night fell on their pleasures, they went home to bed, each to his own lodging. Telemachus’s room was high up in a tower overlooking the outer courtyard, and he went there, brooding and deep in thought. A good old woman, Euryclea, daughter of Ops, the son of Pisenor, went before him with a couple of blazing torches. Laertes had bought her with his own money when she was very young. He gave the price of twenty oxen for her and showed her as much respect in his household as he did his own wedded wife, but he never took her to his bed, because he feared his wife’s resentment. She was the one who now lit Telemachus’s way to his room, and she loved him better than any of the other women in the house did, because she had nursed him as a baby. He opened the door of his bedroom and sat down on the bed. As he took off his shirt, he gave it to the good old woman, who folded it neatly and hung it for him over a peg by his bedside, after which she went out, pulled the door shut with a silver catch, and drew the bolt home with the strap. But Telemachus, lying under a woolen fleece, spent the whole night thinking about his planned voyage and the advice Minerva had given him.
